title: Indian Battery Makers Face Up to 61% Cost Gap With China, NETRA Study Finds
headline: Indian Battery Makers Face Up to 61% Cost Gap With China, NETRA Study Finds

body:
• A NETRA study released by the Ministry of Heavy Industries finds Indian battery component makers face a cost disadvantage of 18% to 61% against landed Chinese prices, depending on the component.
  • The gap is worst in synthetic graphite anodes (61%) and natural graphite (51%), then separators (49%), LFP cathode material (47%), electrolytes (37%), copper foil (27%) and NMC cathode material (18%).
  • Building a cathode plant in India costs 235% more than in China; an anode plant, 425% more. Borrowing runs 8.5–16% against about 3.1% in China.
  • The study offers the government three incentive options — up to a 50% capital subsidy on the semiconductor model — alongside a proposed ₹12,000-crore scheme now under inter-ministerial consultation.

India wants a battery industry that does not run through China. A new study says the arithmetic, for now, runs the other way. "Accelerating India's ACC Component Manufacturing Ecosystem," prepared by NETRA with ARCI, CSIR-NCL, IIT Madras and Deloitte and released by the Ministry of Heavy Industries, finds Indian makers of advanced chemistry cell components face a cost disadvantage of 18% to 61% against landed Chinese benchmark prices, according to pv magazine India.

Where the gap bites

The disadvantage is steepest in the materials India most needs to localise: synthetic graphite anodes at 61%, natural graphite at 51%, separators at 49%, LFP cathode material at 47%, electrolytes at 37%, copper foil at 27% and NMC cathode material at 18%. The causes differ by component — raw material prices for cathodes, electrolytes and copper foil; conversion, energy and financing costs for graphite anodes; capital intensity and low early utilisation for separators. The capital gap is stark: cathode plant capex in India runs 235% above China's, anode capex 425% above, and Indian firms borrow at 8.5–16% against roughly 3.1% in China. China, the study notes, supplied 99% of the world's LFP cathode material and 90% of anode material in 2025.

"The cost data in this report comes from Indian companies that are building or planning these plants, and it shows that the gap has a different cause in each component. A flat incentive would overpay some producers and underpay others."

— Debi Prasad Dash, Co-Founder and Executive Director, NETRA

The ask: three options, not one demand

Rather than a single subsidy demand, the study lays out three options: a 25% capital subsidy plus a sales-linked operating incentive offsetting about 30% of each component's gap; an operating incentive alone covering about 60% of the gap for five to seven years; or a 50% capital subsidy released alongside the investor's own spending, modelled on the Semicon India programme. Each option, the study stresses, leaves manufacturers carrying a meaningful share of the gap. Moneycontrol reports the government is separately preparing a ₹12,000-crore incentive scheme for ACC components, under inter-ministerial consultation, to sit alongside the existing ₹18,100-crore production-linked incentive for cell manufacturing. These are proposals, not approved policy.

Why the timing matters

The demand side is not in doubt: the study projects India's battery demand rising from about 33 GWh in 2025 to 236 GWh in 2032 and close to 600 GWh by 2037, while current Indian capacity covers less than 3% of the cathode, anode and electrolyte supply that 2032 will require — and there is no known domestic production of separators or battery-grade copper foil. NETRA's Dr Rahul Walawalkar put the deadline plainly: "Decisions taken by March 2027 will decide whether the cell plants coming online by March 2029 can buy qualified materials made in India." For diaspora investors, the listed Indian materials makers — the segment's two most established names are Epsilon Advanced Materials and Himadri Speciality Chemical, per the Hindu BusinessLine — are the obvious beneficiaries if the subsidy bridge is built. Until it is, the 61% gap is the story: a forecast of a boom is not the boom.
